transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in today?

Well, I... I suppose I came in because things have just been so strange lately, and I don't really know how else to explain it except that it's just so loud. I live alone, you see, in this little studio apartment over on 4th Street. It’s small, just one room really, with the kitchenette right there when you walk in, so it’s not like there’s anywhere for someone to hide. But I keep hearing these voices. And I mean, they are as clear as day. It’s not like a whisper or a mumble through the walls from the neighbors—I know what Mr. Henderson next door sounds like when his TV is too loud. This is different. This sounds exactly like there is a person standing right there in the room with me, maybe just a few feet away, right by my little dining table. 

They keep saying my name. Just over and over. And then they start telling me that my work is being judged. I work as a personal care aide, you know, going to people's houses, helping them bathe and eat, which is hard work, really hard work, especially on my back. But these voices, they tell me I'm being watched and judged on everything I do. And the most terrifying part is that the house will be completely quiet. I’ll have the TV off, the radio off, just sitting there trying to rest my feet after a long shift, and nobody is there. I’ve checked the locks, I’ve looked in the little closet, I’ve even opened the window to see if someone is on the fire escape, but there’s never anybody there. Yet the voices are just so real, so clear, standing right there in my studio... it's just making it so hard to even think straight anymore.
How long have you been hearing these voices?

Well, let me think... it hasn't just been a few days or a couple of weeks, that's for sure. I remember it started right around the time the weather started getting really cold last year, maybe right after Thanksgiving? Yes, it was definitely after Thanksgiving because I had just bought this heavy winter coat from the thrift store on Main Street, the one with the faux fur collar that keeps my neck so warm when I'm waiting for the bus at 5:00 in the morning. So, if I count back from now... December, January, February... it's been about nine months. 

Nine whole months of this. Nine months of hearing them talk to me, right there in my apartment, and nine months of this... this absolute certainty, this fixed fear that my work is being watched and judged. And it's not just a passing thought, you know? It's like this heavy weight sitting on my chest every single day for nine months. I go into Mrs. Gable's house—she's one of my clients, sweet lady, but she needs a lot of help getting out of bed—and I'm constantly looking over my shoulder, wondering who is taking notes on how I lift her, or how I prepare her oatmeal. It’s exhausting, doctor, just so exhausting to live like this for three-quarters of a year, never having a moment's peace in my own home or at my job, always feeling those eyes on me and hearing those voices judging me...
Have you had a period lasting several days when you felt unusually energized or irritable, needed much less sleep, and were more active or talkative than usual?

Oh, absolutely, yes. There are times, well, sometimes it lasts for days or even a whole week, where I don't even look at my bed. I'll be up all night scrubbing the baseboards in the apartment, completely rearranging my little kitchenette, and I don't feel tired at all when the sun comes up. I actually feel... well, it's hard to describe, but I go from feeling so incredibly bright, like I'm glowing from the inside out, and just so chosen, you know? Like I have this grand, special purpose. And when I get like that, Greenville just feels so tiny. I mean, Greenville can’t even begin to hold all my plans. I have so many ideas, so many things I need to do, and I'll just talk and talk to anyone who will listen—the bus driver, the cashier at the grocery store—because my mind is just racing with all these brilliant thoughts. 

But then... then it changes. It doesn't just fade away, it twists. I'll still have all that buzzing energy, but instead of feeling wonderful, I get so wound up and angry. I'll end up snapping hard at someone over just a tiny, small thing. Like just last week, one of my clients, sweet lady, she just didn't hear me when I said I was going to heat up her soup, and she asked me to repeat myself. Just a simple question, right? But I just snapped at her. I bit her head off over absolutely nothing because my skin was just crawling and I couldn't stand being asked the same thing twice. I felt terrible about it later, I really did, because that's not how I want to treat people, but in those days when I'm all keyed up and not sleeping, it's like a switch flips from being on top of the world to just being so agitated that I can't even stand the sound of my own breathing.
Have you ever continued hearing the voices during a period when you were not feeling unusually energized, irritable, or depressed?

Well, yes... yes, actually. I know exactly what you mean because it was so confusing to me when it happened. You see, after that whole period where I was just buzzing around, scrubbing the baseboards and snapping at poor Mrs. Gable—which, like I said, I still feel just awful about because she really is a dear, she just can't hear very well out of her left ear since she had that infection last spring. But anyway, after all that energy finally ran out, and it always does, it's like a balloon just deflating all at once. I crashed. I went back to sleeping, you know, a normal amount. I wasn't staying up all night rearranging the kitchenette anymore. I was actually sleeping through the night, maybe seven or eight hours, waking up feeling tired but not that awful, heavy, can't-get-out-of-bed kind of tired. Just... normal tired. My mood was fine. I wasn't angry, I wasn't on top of the world. I was just me again, just going to work and coming home to my little studio on 4th Street.

But the thing is, doctor, the voices didn't stop. They didn't even quiet down. I thought maybe when I finally got some sleep, my head would clear, but no. For weeks—I'd say it was at least three or four weeks of me just feeling completely normal, mood-wise—they were still there. Standing right by the dining table, saying my name over and over. And that awful feeling, that absolute certainty that people were watching me and judging every single thing I did at work, taking notes on how I helped my clients... that stayed, too. It was just as strong as ever. I'd be making a sandwich for lunch, feeling perfectly calm, no racing thoughts, no anger, and yet there they were, telling me I was being evaluated. It went on like that for several weeks, just this steady stream of voices and being watched, even though the rest of me, my energy and my mood, felt completely level. It just doesn't make any sense, does it? How can I feel so normal in one way, but still have all that going on?
Have you used alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, hallucinogens, or any other non-prescribed drugs around the times when the voices and beliefs began or worsened?

Oh, heavens, no. No, no, no. I don't touch any of that. Not a drop, not a puff, nothing. I mean, I think I might have had half a glass of cheap champagne at my niece's wedding, but that was... oh, Lord, that must have been six or seven years ago now? Yes, because she just had her second baby right before Christmas. But as for everyday life, or when all this started with the voices and the feeling like I'm being watched? Absolutely not. 

I don't drink, and I certainly don't do any drugs or marijuana or whatever else people are doing these days. Working as a personal care aide, you know, you see things. I've been in homes where family members have ruined their whole lives over a bottle or a pill, and I just promised myself I'd never go down that road. Plus, on my salary? I barely make enough to keep the lights on in my little studio on 4th Street and buy my groceries, let alone spend it on something foolish like that. I wouldn't even know where to buy a... a hallucinogen if my life depended on it! I mean, who even sells that? Greenville is just too small, or maybe I'm just too old for that crowd. I wouldn't even know who to ask.

And really, doctor, my stomach is so sensitive anyway. If I even have a second cup of coffee in the morning—the regular kind, not the decaf I usually buy in that little green tin at the Piggly Wiggly—I get this terrible heartburn that just sits right here in the middle of my chest all afternoon. So no, I haven't taken anything. I don't take anything not prescribed to me. I need all my wits about me just to get through the day with those people evaluating my work and the voices constantly talking at me, you know? It takes everything I have just to focus on making Mrs. Gable's oatmeal without dropping the bowl. I couldn't imagine clouding up my head with drugs or alcohol on top of all this mess, it just wouldn't make a lick of sense. So no, definitely not.

During those periods of very little sleep, racing thoughts, and feeling unusually powerful, did your behavior cause serious problems at work or in relationships, require hospitalization, or make you unable to function normally?

Oh, it definitely caused problems. I mean, it really made a mess of things, more than I care to admit. You know I work as a personal care aide, and I've always prided myself on being reliable. I've been doing this for a long time, and my clients depend on me. But when I get like that, with my mind just going a mile a minute and feeling so... so full of myself, I suppose... well, my job was actually in real danger. 

I started missing my shifts entirely. I'd just completely forget I was supposed to be at a client's house by 8 AM because I was too busy doing something else, like rewriting all my recipes onto new index cards or something foolish like that. And the paperwork! We have to keep very strict logs, you know—what they ate, when they took their pills, if they had a bowel movement—it's very detailed work. But I was mixing up all my care notes. I'd write one person's information on another person's chart, or my handwriting would just be this frantic scribble that nobody could read. I just could not keep my visits organized the way I used to. I was showing up at the wrong times, double-booking myself, or just not showing up at all. My supervisor had to call me in to the office, and she was not happy, not one bit. She told me if I didn't get it together, they'd have to let me go, which terrified me because I need this job.

And it wasn't just work, either. It bled into my personal life, too. I used to try to be somewhat social, you know, to get out of the apartment. I had this walking club I went to every Tuesday and Thursday morning over at the park, just a nice group of ladies my age, and we'd walk the loop twice and chat. And I also really loved going to the downtown library for these art talks they put on every month—they bring in a little projector and show slides of famous paintings, and it's just really lovely and quiet. 

But during all that time when I was so wound up, I just stopped going to all of it. I stopped going to the walking club, I completely dropped out of the library art talks. I don't even know why exactly... I think maybe my head was just too full of my own big plans, or I just couldn't sit still long enough to listen to someone talk about a painting when I felt like I had to be doing a hundred other things. But the result was that I ended up just being mostly alone at home. Just me, pacing around my little studio, messing up my work schedule and isolating myself from everyone I actually enjoyed spending time with. So yes, it made it nearly impossible to just live my normal life.
During the weeks when you felt emotionally normal but continued hearing the voices and believing you were being watched, was there any time when those symptoms stopped completely?

Stopped? Oh, heavens, no. I wish they had. I really, really wish they had, because that would have given me some peace, wouldn't it? But no, they never stopped. Not once. It's like having a television left on in the next room that you just can't unplug, no matter what you do. 

Even when my mood completely leveled out and I was just, you know, going about my normal business, getting up, making my toast, getting ready for work... they were still there. In fact, if I really sit down and think about it—and believe me, doctor, I have, I've sat at my little table on 4th Street for hours just trying to trace it all back to figure out when my life turned so upside down—the voices and those awful, fixed fears about my work being watched, well, they have been happening for about nine months now. 

Nine whole months! Can you imagine? It feels like a lifetime. That's almost a whole year of hearing people talking at you and feeling that absolute dread that someone is hiding just out of sight, taking notes on every little thing you do with your clients. Nine months of looking over my shoulder while I'm just trying to do my job and be a good aide. You'd think there would be a break, maybe just one quiet Sunday afternoon, especially when I finally started sleeping again and felt like myself, but no. It hasn't let up for a single day in all these nine months. It just keeps going and going, and I keep waiting for the quiet, but it never comes.

My supervisor had to call me in to the office, and she was not happy, not one bit. She told me if I didn't get it together, they'd have to let me go, which terrified me because I need this job.

And it wasn't just work, either. It bled into my personal life, too. I used to try to be somewhat social, you know, to get out of the apartment. I had this walking club I went to every Tuesday and Thursday morning over at the park, just a nice group of ladies my age, and we'd walk the loop twice and chat. And I also really loved going to the downtown library for these art talks they put on every month—they bring in a little projector and show slides of famous paintings, and it's just really lovely and quiet. 

But during all that time when I was so wound up, I just stopped going to all of it. I stopped going to the walking club, I completely dropped out of the library art talks. I don't even know why exactly... I think maybe my head was just too full of my own big plans, or I just couldn't sit still long enough to listen to someone talk about a painting when I felt like I had to be doing a hundred other things. But the result was that I ended up just being mostly alone at home. Just me, pacing around my little studio, messing up my work schedule and isolating myself from everyone I actually enjoyed spending time with. So yes, it made it nearly impossible to just live my normal life.

inference.note: Persistent hallucinations and delusions for several weeks during euthymia, plus clear impairing manic episodes, support schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.0) versus bipolar disorder with psychotic features (F31.9). Substance-induced and unspecified psychotic disorders are less likely given the reported absence of substance use and established mood episodes.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the psychotic symptoms occur independently of mood episodes for at least two weeks, distinguishing schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: During the weeks when you felt emotionally normal but continued hearing the voices and believing you were being watched, was there any time when those symptoms stopped completely?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and fixed fears about my work being watched have been happening for about 9 months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the continuity and duration of the psychotic symptoms (voices and beliefs of being watched), which directly corresponds to the duration of my psychotic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Stopped? Oh, heavens, no. I wish they had. I really, really wish they had, because that would have given me some peace, wouldn't it? But no, they never stopped. Not once. It's like having a television left on in the next room that you just can't unplug, no matter what you do. 

Even when my mood completely leveled out and I was just, you know, going about my normal business, getting up, making my toast, getting ready for work... they were still there. In fact, if I really sit down and think about it—and believe me, doctor, I have, I've sat at my little table on 4th Street for hours just trying to trace it all back to figure out when my life turned so upside down—the voices and those awful, fixed fears about my work being watched, well, they have been happening for about nine months now. 

Nine whole months! Can you imagine? It feels like a lifetime. That's almost a whole year of hearing people talking at you and feeling that absolute dread that someone is hiding just out of sight, taking notes on every little thing you do with your clients. Nine months of looking over my shoulder while I'm just trying to do my job and be a good aide. You'd think there would be a break, maybe just one quiet Sunday afternoon, especially when I finally started sleeping again and felt like myself, but no. It hasn't let up for a single day in all these nine months. It just keeps going and going, and I keep waiting for the quiet, but it never comes.

inference.note: Persistent hallucinations and delusions for several weeks during euthymic periods support schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type over bipolar I disorder with psychotic features.
